vignette:
Marcus Webb was twenty-six years old when he arrived in South Sudan as a relief worker for an international humanitarian organization. He had spent two years in graduate school studying development economics before deciding that classroom work felt too distant from suffering that felt urgent and real. He was idealistic, physically fit, and believed his presence mattered. For eight months, he distributed medical supplies, helped coordinate food aid in camps swollen with displaced families, and documented conditions for reports that would circulate through offices in New York and Geneva. He was good at the work—calm under pressure, organized, trusted by colleagues. He had no prior trauma history, no anxiety disorder, no reason to think his mind would fracture the way it did.

The attack came on a Tuesday morning in March. Marcus was in a compound with three colleagues when armed men breached the gate. The firefight lasted perhaps ninety seconds. His supervisor was killed. A colleague was shot in the leg. Marcus and the fourth worker barricaded themselves in a storage room where they remained for four hours, listening to voices outside, footsteps, the sound of things being overturned. The gunfire had stopped, but he couldn't know if the men were still there. When peacekeeping forces finally entered, Marcus emerged into daylight that felt obscene in its ordinariness. He was evacuated within twelve hours.

For the first month home in Portland, Marcus functioned. He debriefed with his organization's counselor, filed incident reports, attended a welcome-back dinner where colleagues treated him as if he had returned from a normal rotation. But by week six, something had shifted. His heart would suddenly begin racing—not from exertion, but from nothing he could identify. He would be sitting at his jeweler's bench, carefully setting a diamond, when his chest would tighten and his pulse would hammer against his ribs. The sensation itself became terrifying. Each time it happened, he was certain something terrible was about to occur, though nothing ever did. He began checking his pulse obsessively, convinced the irregularity meant he was having a heart attack. He visited an emergency room twice. Both times, the cardiologist found nothing wrong. Now, at twenty-nine, three years after the compound attack, Marcus still found himself reaching for his wrist in the middle of ordinary moments, waiting to feel the skip or surge that would confirm his worst fear—that his body was betraying him in ways he couldn't control or predict. He had come to believe that his mind was broken in a way that couldn't be fixed—that he had seen something that had fundamentally altered his capacity to feel secure anywhere.

The sounds were worse. A child crying in a grocery store would stop him mid-aisle. Not the mild distress of a tired toddler, but any child's cry—it would transport him completely. He would hear not the Portland supermarket but the compound, the camp, the particular pitch of a young girl who had been brought to the medical tent with a fever, whose mother had wept while Marcus held the child's hand. He stopped going to stores during school hours. He began doing his shopping at midnight. What terrified Marcus most was that he could no longer trust his own assessment of safety. Logically, he knew he was in Portland, in America, in a city where nothing was happening. But his body didn't believe it. He had come to believe that his mind was broken in a way that couldn't be fixed—that he had seen something that had fundamentally altered his capacity to feel secure anywhere. He began positioning himself with his back against walls, a habit so ingrained now that he felt exposed and vulnerable sitting any other way. At his jeweler's bench, he had rearranged his workspace so he could see the shop entrance while working. His boss had noticed the change but hadn't commented. When he slept, his dreams were vivid and fragmented—not coherent replays but distorted scenes where the storage room had no walls, where his supervisor's voice called to him from places that made no spatial sense, where he was running but his legs wouldn't move. He would wake gasping, his sheets soaked, his heart still racing from the dream logic that felt more real than waking.

The hypervigilance had become exhausting. Marcus found himself constantly scanning rooms for potential weapons—the letter opener on a desk, a heavy stapler, the way a person held their hands. In his apartment, he had begun noting which objects could be used as weapons, which exits were available, where the blind spots were. He knew this was irrational. He also couldn't stop. When his memories surfaced, they felt more vivid and real than anything in his present life. A memory of the storage room—the specific smell of fertilizer and diesel fuel, the texture of concrete against his back, the exact timbre of his colleague's breathing—would arrive unbidden and complete, as if he were there again rather than remembering. Sometimes the emotional intensity would come without any image at all: pure terror and helplessness, flooding through him with no narrative attached, leaving him gasping and confused about why he felt such overwhelming dread. Marcus had tried to manage this by reminding himself that things could have been worse—he was alive, his colleagues had survived, the organization had reopened the compound. He forced himself to think positive thoughts, to focus on the good work he had done, the lives he had helped. But these strategies felt hollow. The symptoms had not diminished.

Three months ago, his supervisor had gently suggested that Marcus take a leave from the bench work. He was making mistakes—a stone had been set slightly off-center on a custom engagement ring, something that would have been unthinkable before. Marcus had agreed, and now he worked in the shop's administrative side, processing orders and managing inventory. He hated it. He felt diminished by it, as if the attack had taken not just his peace of mind but his competence, his identity as the careful craftsman he had always been. Last week, a colleague had touched his shoulder without warning—a simple gesture of greeting. Marcus had flinched violently, his entire body tensing. The colleague had apologized, confused by the reaction. That moment crystallized something for Marcus: he was no longer the person he had been. He didn't know how to live in his own body anymore. He called a therapist yesterday and scheduled an intake for next week. He is terrified that nothing will help, but he is more terrified of continuing as he is—trapped between the memory of who he was and the frightened, fractured man he has become.
